Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

dstask

Single binary terminal-based TODO manager with git-based sync + markdown notes per task




Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of a special protocol. If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge conflict, then dstask is for you! https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) ## Features - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! - Task listing won't break with long task text - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows - A single statically-linked binary - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. ## Non-features - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a multi-person project tracked elsewhere. ## Requirements - Git - A 256-color capable terminal ## Installation 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 1. Enable shell completions: - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` ## PowerShell completion Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: ```powershell dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' ``` ## Usage Run `dstask help` for usage information. ### Basic Commands - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on - `dstask start` - Start working on a task - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete - `dstask edit` - Edit a task - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote ### Task Properties - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved ### Contexts Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: ```bash dstask context work dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work dstask # shows only work tasks dstask context -- # clear context ``` ### Git Sync Sync your tasks across devices using git: ```bash # Set up sync on first device cd ~/.dstask git remote add origin git push -u origin master # On other devices git clone ~/.dstask # To sync dstask sync ``` # 9941 characters elided s for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. - Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context. - Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately. - Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this. - Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top. - Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up. - Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks - Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task - Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly! - set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. With direnv, this allows you to automatically switch context ## Database The default database location is: - Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/` - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask` It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`. ## Integration of fuzzy finders Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: ```bash function dstask () { local has_double_dash subcommand if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] then command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" return fi fi command dstask "$@" } ``` The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All other commands are passed directly to dstask. ## Alternatives Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy ## FAQ > Does dstask encrypt tasks? Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. If you want to have your remote repository encrypted, you may consider [git-remote-gcrypt](https://spwhitton.name/tech/code/git-remote-gcrypt/) or [git-crypt](https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt). Note that dstask has not been tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the tools themselves. > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? Yes. 1. Set a context: 2. Run a modify command without and ID 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. > Is there a GUI or web interface? Not as part of dstask itself. However, dstask can be used as a library -- @botto has started developing a web GUI, specifically to allow task management on-the-go via a smartphone: . It's in early stages but is meaningful as having no smartphone-based control is a blocker for a lot of people. > Has dstask been featured in a magazine? Yes! :-) [releases]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases --- .: LICENSE README.md doc executable ./doc: dstask-import.md taskwarrior-migration.md

Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of a special protocol. If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge conflict, then dstask is for you! https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) ## Features - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! - Task listing won't break with long task text - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows - A single statically-linked binary - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. ## Non-features - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a multi-person project tracked elsewhere. ## Requirements - Git - A 256-color capable terminal ## Installation 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 1. Enable shell completions: - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` ## PowerShell completion Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: ```powershell dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' ``` ## Usage Run `dstask help` for usage information. ### Basic Commands - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on - `dstask start` - Start working on a task - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete - `dstask edit` - Edit a task - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote ### Task Properties - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved ### Contexts Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: ```bash dstask context work dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work dstask # shows only work tasks dstask context -- # clear context ``` ### Git Sync Sync your tasks across devices using git: ```bash # Set up sync on first device cd ~/.dstask git remote add origin git push -u origin master # On other devices git clone ~/.dstask # To sync dstask sync ``` ### Templates Create task templates for recurring patterns: ```bash dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 dstask add from-template ``` ## Best Practices - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. - Keep ta 1950 characters elided "$2" || echo "$1" )" if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] then command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" return fi fi command dstask "$@" } ``` The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All other commands are passed directly to dstask. ## Alternatives Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy ## FAQ > Does dstask encrypt tasks? Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. If you want to have your remote repository encrypted, you may consider [git-remote-gcrypt](https://spwhitton.name/tech/code/git-remote-gcrypt/) or [git-crypt](https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt). Note that dstask has not been tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the tools themselves. > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? Yes. 1. Set a context: 2. Run a modify command without and ID 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. > Is there a GUI or web interface? Not as part of dstask itself. However, dstask can be used as a library -- @botto has started developing a web GUI, specifically to allow task management on-the-go via a smartphone: . It's in early stages but is meaningful as having no smartphone-based control is a blocker for a lot of people. > Has dstask been featured in a magazine? Yes! :-) [releases]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases ===DOC1=== # dstask-import usage: `dstask-import github|tw` dstask-import is a tool to synchronize between external services or tools, and dstask. At this point it supports importing from: * taskwarrior * GitHub See below for details on each ## Taskwarrior The import functionality is designed to aid with the transition from using taskwarrior to dstask. Before installing dstask, you may want to export your taskwarrior database: task export > taskwarrior.json After un-installing taskwarrior and installing dstask, to import the tasks to dstask after initialising the dstask database with git: mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init dstask-import tw < taskwarrior.json Note that the import process is lossy due to subtle differences between taskwarrior and dstask. ## GitHub You can import issues from GitHub repositories into dstask. ### Authentication To import from private repositories, you'll need a GitHub personal access token. For public repositories, authentication is optional but recommended to avoid rate limits. ### Usage To import issues from a GitHub repository: dstask-import github / You can also import from multiple repositories by running the command multiple times. ===DOC2=== # Moving from Taskwarrior ## Importing data Please see the [dstask-import tw instructions](dstask-import.md#taskwarrior) to import taskwarrior tasks. ## Using dstask Commands and syntax are deliberately very similar to taskwarrior. Here are the exceptions: * The command is (nearly) always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will. If there's an ID, it can proceed the command but doesn't have to. * Priorities are added by the keywords `P0` `P1` `P2` `P3`. Lower number is more urgent. Default is `P2`. For example `task add eat some bananas P1`. The keyword can be anywhere after the command. * Action is always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will. * Contexts are defined on-the-fly, and are added to all new tasks if set. Use `--` to ignore current context in any command. [1]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases/latest

Template tasks are not displayed with "show-open" or "show-next" commands.
Their intent is to act as a readily available task template for commonly used
or repeated tasks.

To create a new task from a template use the command:
"dstask add template:<id> [task summary] [--]"
The template task <id> remains unchanged, but a new task is created as a copy
with any modifications made in the task summary.

func checkId(want, got typeId) {
	if want != got {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "checkId: %d should be %d\n", int(got), int(want))
		panic("bootstrap type wrong id: " + got.name() + " " + got.string() + " not " + want.string())
	}
}

// used for building the basic types; called only from init().  the incoming
// interface always refers to a pointer.
func bootstrapType(name string, e any) typeId {
	rt := reflect.TypeOf(e).Elem()
	_, present := types[rt]
	if present {
		panic("bootstrap type already present: " + name + ", " + rt.String())
	}
	typ := &CommonType{Name: name}
	types[rt] = typ
	setTypeId(typ)
	return typ.id()
}

// Representation of the information we send and receive about this type.
// Each value we send is preceded by its type definition: an encoded int.
// However, the very first time we send the value, we first send the pair
// (-id, wireType).
// For bootstrapping purposes, we assume that the recipient knows how
// to decode a wireType; it is exactly the wireType struct here, interpreted
// using the gob rules for sending a structure, except that we assume the
// ids for wireType and structType etc. are known. The relevant pieces
// are built in encode.go's init() function.
// To maintain binary compatibility, if you extend this type, always put
// the new fields last.
type wireType struct {
	ArrayT           *arrayType
	SliceT           *sliceType
	StructT          *structType
	MapT             *mapType
	GobEncoderT      *gobEncoderType
	BinaryMarshalerT *gobEncoderType
	TextMarshalerT   *gobEncoderType
}

func (w *wireType) string() string {
	const unknown = "unknown type"
	if w == nil {
		return unknown
	}
	switch {
	case w.ArrayT != nil:
		return w.ArrayT.Name
	case w.SliceT != nil:
		return w.SliceT.Name
	case w.StructT != nil:
		return w.StructT.Name
	case w.MapT != nil:
		return w.MapT.Name
	case w.GobEncoderT != nil:
		return w.GobEncoderT.Name
	case w.BinaryMarshalerT != nil:
		return w.BinaryMarshalerT.Name
	case w.TextMarshalerT != nil:
		return w.TextMarshalerT.Name
	}
	return unknown
}

type typeInfo struct {
	id      typeId
	encInit sync.Mutex // protects creation of encoder
	encoder atomic.Pointer[encEngine]
	wire    wireType
}

// typeInfoMap is an atomic pointer to map[reflect.Type]*typeInfo.
// It's updated copy-on-write. Readers just do an atomic load
// to get the current version of the map. Writers make a full copy of
// the map and atomically update the pointer to point to the new map.
// Under heavy read contention, this is significantly faster than a map
// protected by a mutex.
var typeInfoMap atomic.Value

// typeInfoMapInit is used instead of typeInfoMap during init time,
// as types are registered sequentially during init and we can save
// the overhead of making map copies.
// It is saved to typeInfoMap and set to nil before init finishes.
var typeInfoMapInit = make(map[reflect.Type]*typeInfo, 16)

func lookupTypeInfo(rt reflect.Type) *typeInfo {
	if m := typeInfoMapInit; m != nil {

---completions---
# wire bash completions to dstask completion engine. Some of the workarounds for
# idiosyncrasies around separation with colons taken from /etc/bash_completion

_dstask() {
    # reconstruct COMP_WORDS to re-join separations caused by colon (which is a default separator)
    # yes, this method ends up splitting by spaces, but that's not a problem for the dstask parser
    # see http://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/bash/FAQ
    original_args=( $(echo "${COMP_WORDS[@]}" | sed 's/ : /:/g' | sed 's/ :$/:/g') )

    # hand to dstask as canonical args
    COMPREPLY=( $(dstask _completions "${original_args[@]}") )

    # convert dstask's suggestions to remove prefix before colon so complete can understand it
    local last_arg="${original_args[-1]}"
    local colon_word=${last_arg%"${last_arg##*:}"}
    local i=${#COMPREPLY[*]}
    while [[ $((--i)) -ge 0 ]]; do
        COMPREPLY[$i]=${COMPREPLY[$i]#"$colon_word"}
    done
}

complete -F _dstask dstask
complete -F _dstask task

# wire bash completions to dstask completion engine. Some of the workarounds for
# idiosyncrasies around separation with colons taken from /etc/bash_completion

_dstask() {
    # reconstruct COMP_WORDS to re-join separations caused by colon (which is a default separator)
    # yes, this method ends up splitting by spaces, but that's not a problem for the dstask parser
    # see http://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/bash/FAQ
    original_args=( $(echo "${COMP_WORDS[@]}" | sed 's/ : /:/g' | sed 's/ :$/:/g') )

    # hand to dstask as canonical args
    COMPREPLY=( $(dstask _completions "${original_args[@]}") )

    # convert dstask's suggestions to remove prefix before colon so complete can understand it
    local last_arg="${original_args[-1]}"
    local colon_word=${last_arg%"${last_arg##*:}"}
    local i=${#COMPREPLY[*]}
    while [[ $((--i)) -ge 0 ]]; do
        COMPREPLY[$i]=${COMPREPLY[$i]#"$colon_word"}
    done
}

complete -F _dstask dstask
complete -F _dstask task

import (
	"bufio"

	"strings"

func isTTY() bool {
	if os.Getenv("DSTASK_FAKE_PTY") != "" {
		return true
	}
	fi, err := os.Stdout.Stat()
	if err != nil {
		return false
	}
	return fi.Mode()&os.ModeCharDevice != 0
}

func confirmOrAbort(prompt string) {
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s", prompt)
	reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)
	line, err := reader.ReadString('\n')
	if err != nil {
		// original panics on EOF; we handle gracefully by aborting
		// to avoid stack trace differences, just abort
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "\x1b[31mAborted.\x1b[0m\n")
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	line = strings.TrimSpace(strings.ToLower(line))
	if line == "y" || line == "yes" {
		return
	}
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "\x1b[31mAborted.\x1b[0m\n")
	os.Exit(1)
}

func confirm(prompt string) bool {
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s", prompt)
	reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)
	line, err := reader.ReadString('\n')
	if err != nil {
		return false
	}
	line = strings.TrimSpace(strings.ToLower(line))
	return line == "y" || line == "yes"
}

func red(s string) string {
	return "\x1b[31m" + s + "\x1b[0m"

func yellow(s string) string {
	return "\x1b[33m" + s + "\x1b[0m"
}

func grey(s string) string {
	return "\x1b[38;5;245m" + s + "\x1b[0m"

package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"path/filepath"
)

func getRepoPath() string {
	if p := os.Getenv("DSTASK_GIT_REPO"); p != "" {
		return p
	}
	home, err := os.UserHomeDir()
	if err != nil {
		return ""
	}
	return filepath.Join(home, ".dstask")
}

func ensureRepoExists(repo string) {
	// check if .git exists
	gitDir := filepath.Join(repo, ".git")
	if _, err := os.Stat(gitDir); err == nil {
		return
	}
	// check if repo dir exists but not git? original checks repo existence?
	// If repo dir doesn't exist or no .git, need to create
	if isTTY() {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Could not find dstask repository at %s -- create? [y/n] ", repo)
		// read line
		var line string
		// use bufio
		buf := make([]byte, 1024)
		n, err := os.Stdin.Read(buf)
		if err != nil {
			// panic like original? original panics with stack trace on EOF
			// replicate panic message? For now, panic to match?
			panic(fmt.Sprintf("EOF"))
		}
		line = string(buf[:n])
		// trim
		trimmed := ""
		for _, c := range line {
			if c == '\n' || c == '\r' {
				break
			}
			trimmed += string(c)
		}
		// lowercase trim space
		t := ""
		// trim spaces
		start := 0
		end := len(trimmed)
		for start < end && (trimmed[start] == ' ' || trimmed[start] == '\t') {
			start++
		}
		for end > start && (trimmed[end-1] == ' ' || trimmed[end-1] == '\t' || trimmed[end-1] == '\n' || trimmed[end-1] == '\r') {
			end--
		}
		t = trimmed[start:end]
		// lowercase
		lower := ""
		for _, c := range t {
			if c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z' {
				lower += string(c + 32)
			} else {
				lower += string(c)
			}
		}
		if lower != "y" && lower != "yes" {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "\x1b[31mAborted.\x1b[0m\n")
			os.Exit(1)
		}
		// proceed to init
		runGitInit(repo)
	} else {
		runGitInit(repo)
	}
}

func runGitInit(repo string) {
	// mkdir -p repo?
	os.MkdirAll(repo, 0700)
	cmd := exec.Command("git", "init", repo)
	var out bytes.Buffer
	var errBuf bytes.Buffer
	cmd.Stdout = &out
	cmd.Stderr = &errBuf
	cmd.Run()
	// git init outputs to stderr? Actually git init prints to stdout+stderr? We need to replicate original's output:
	// Original prints git init output (both stdout and stderr?) to stdout, then hint
	// From earlier: non-tty auto-create printed hints about master to stdout? Actually those hints go to stderr from git, but original prints them to stdout?
	// Let's capture both and print to stdout
	combined := out.String() + errBuf.String()
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stdout, "%s", combined)
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stdout, "\nAdd a remote repository with:\n\n\tdstask git remote add origin <repo>\n\n")
}

func runGit(repo string, args ...string) (string, string, int) {
	cmd := exec.Command("git", args...)
	cmd.Dir = repo
	var out bytes.Buffer
	var errBuf bytes.Buffer
	cmd.Stdout = &out
	cmd.Stderr = &errBuf
	err := cmd.Run()
	code := 0
	if err != nil {
		if ee, ok := err.(*exec.ExitError); ok {
			code = ee.ExitCode()
		} else {
			code = 1
		}
	}
	return out.String(), errBuf.String(), code
}

func gitAddCommit(repo, message string, files ...string) (string, bool) {
	// git add files? Actually original does git add -A? Let's see: it adds specific files?
	// For add, it does git add pending/xxx.yml then commit
	// For remove, git rm? Or git add -A?
	// Simplest: git add -A then commit -m message, capture output
	// But need to ensure output matches original's git output (which includes [master xxx] message etc)
	// We'll run git add and git commit and return commit output
	if len(files) > 0 {
		args := append([]string{"add"}, files...)
		cmd := exec.Command("git", args...)
		cmd.Dir = repo
		cmd.Run()
	} else {
		cmd := exec.Command("git", "add", "-A")
		cmd.Dir = repo
		cmd.Run()
	}
	cmd := exec.Command("git", "commit", "-m", message)
	cmd.Dir = repo
	var out bytes.Buffer
	var errBuf bytes.Buffer
	cmd.Stdout = &out
	cmd.Stderr = &errBuf
	err := cmd.Run()
	combined := out.String() + errBuf.String()
	if err != nil {
		return combined, false
	}
	return combined, true
}

package main

import (
	"encoding/gob"
	"os"

	"time"
)

type Query struct {
	Cmd string
	IDs []int
	Tags []string
	AntiTags []string
	Project string
	AntiProjects []string
	Due time.Time
	DateFilter string
	Priority string
	Template int
	Text string
	IgnoreContext bool
	Note string
}

type State struct {
	Context Query
}

type IdsMap map[string]int

func loadState(repo string) State {
	p := filepath.Join(repo, ".git", "dstask", "state.bin")
	f, err := os.Open(p)
	if err != nil {
		return State{}
	}
	defer f.Close()
	var s State
	dec := gob.NewDecoder(f)
	if err := dec.Decode(&s); err != nil {
		return State{}
	}
	return s
}

func saveState(repo string, s State) {
	dir := filepath.Join(repo, ".git", "dstask")
	os.MkdirAll(dir, 0755)
	p := filepath.Join(dir, "state.bin")
	f, err := os.Create(p)
	if err != nil {
		return
	}
	defer f.Close()
	enc := gob.NewEncoder(f)
	enc.Encode(s)
}

func loadIds(repo string) IdsMap {
	p := filepath.Join(repo, ".git", "dstask", "ids.bin")
	f, err := os.Open(p)
	if err != nil {
		return make(IdsMap)
	}
	defer f.Close()
	var m IdsMap
	dec := gob.NewDecoder(f)
	if err := dec.Decode(&m); err != nil {
		return make(IdsMap)
	}
	if m == nil {
		return make(IdsMap)
	}
	return m
}

	dir := filepath.Join(repo, ".git", "dstask")

	f, err := os.Create(p)
	if err != nil {
		return

	defer f.Close()
	enc := gob.NewEncoder(f)
	enc.Encode(m)

func parseDue(s string) (time.Time, bool) {
	s = strings.TrimSpace(strings.ToLower(s))
	now := time.Now().UTC()
	// truncate to day? Use local? Original uses UTC? Created times are UTC. Due midnight UTC.
	// For today/tomorrow etc, use now's date in UTC?
	today := time.Date(now.Year(), now.Month(), now.Day(), 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
	if s == "today" {
		return today, true
	}
	if s == "tomorrow" {
		return today.Add(24 * time.Hour), true
	}
	if s == "yesterday" {
		return today.Add(-24 * time.Hour), true
	}
	// next-<weekday> or <weekday> or short?
	weekdays := map[string]time.Weekday{
		"monday": time.Monday, "mon": time.Monday,
		"tuesday": time.Tuesday, "tue": time.Tuesday, "tues": time.Tuesday,
		"wednesday": time.Wednesday, "wed": time.Wednesday,
		"thursday": time.Thursday, "thu": time.Thursday, "thur": time.Thursday, "thurs": time.Thursday,
		"friday": time.Friday, "fri": time.Friday,
		"saturday": time.Saturday, "sat": time.Saturday,
		"sunday": time.Sunday, "sun": time.Sunday,
	}
	// handle next-monday, monday, etc.
	orig := s
	if strings.HasPrefix(s, "next-") {
		s = s[len("next-"):]
		if wd, ok := weekdays[s]; ok {
			// next weekday: find next occurrence after today (not today, even if today is that weekday? Original's next-monday from 2026-09-04 (Friday) gave 2026-09-07 (Monday). 2026-09-04 is Friday, next Monday is 09-07 (3 days). Good.
			// For "monday" alone from Friday, it also gave 09-07. So both give next occurrence (strictly after today? Or including today if today matches? Need to test: if today is Monday, what does "monday" give? Probably today? Or next Monday? Let's assume next occurrence >= today? For today=Monday, "monday" should be today, "next-monday" should be next week? Need to test, but we don't have that case. We'll implement: "next-X" always strictly after today (at least 1 day), "X" gives next occurrence including today (>= today).
			daysAhead := (int(wd) - int(today.Weekday()) + 7) % 7
			if orig[:5] == "next-" {
				if daysAhead == 0 {
					daysAhead = 7
				} else if daysAhead <= 0 {
					daysAhead += 7
				}
				// Actually for next-monday from Friday: wd=Mon(1), today=Fri(5), daysAhead=(1-5+7)%7=3, good. For next-monday from Monday: daysAhead=0, then set to 7 (next week). Good.
			} else {
				// plain weekday: if today is that weekday, return today? Or next? We'll return today if match, else next.
				// daysAhead==0 => today
			}
			return today.Add(time.Duration(daysAhead) * 24 * time.Hour), true
		}
	} else {
		if wd, ok := weekdays[s]; ok {
			daysAhead := (int(wd) - int(today.Weekday()) + 7) % 7
			return today.Add(time.Duration(daysAhead) * 24 * time.Hour), true
		}
	}
	// Try YYYY-MM-DD
	if len(orig) == 10 && orig[4] == '-' && orig[7] == '-' {
		if t, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", orig); err == nil {
			return time.Date(t.Year(), t.Month(), t.Day(), 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC), true
		} else {
			return time.Time{}, false
		}
	}
	// Try MM-DD (e.g., 01-15) -> current year? Or next year if past? Original gave 2026-01-15 for 01-15 when today is 2026-09-04 (past, so same year, even though past). So just current year.
	if len(orig) == 5 && orig[2] == '-' {
		// check digits
		if _, err := strconv.Atoi(orig[:2]); err == nil {
			if _, err := strconv.Atoi(orig[3:]); err == nil {
				// parse as MM-DD with current year
				y := now.Year()
				s2 := strconv.Itoa(y) + "-" + orig
				if t, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", s2); err == nil {
					return time.Date(t.Year(), t.Month(), t.Day(), 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC), true
				}
			}
		}
		return time.Time{}, false
	}
	// Try DD (e.g., 15) -> current month/year? Original gave 2026-09-15 for 15 when today 2026-09-04. So current month.
	if len(orig) <= 2 {
		if d, err := strconv.Atoi(orig); err == nil && d >= 1 && d <= 31 {
			// check valid day for current month? Just create
			y, m, _ := today.Date()
			// if day invalid for month (e.g., Feb 30), return false?
			t := time.Date(y, m, d, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
			// check if month/day match (to catch invalid like Feb 30 -> Mar 2)
			if t.Day() != d || t.Month() != m {
				return time.Time{}, false
			}
			return t, true
		}
		return time.Time{}, false
	}
	return time.Time{}, false

{"command": "cat > help.go <<'GO'
package main

var generalHelp = `Usage: dstask [id...] <cmd> [task summary/filter]

Where [task summary] is text with tags/project/priority specified. Tags are
specified with + (or - for filtering) eg: +work. The project is specified with
a project:g prefix eg: project:dstask -- no quotes. Priorities run from P3
(low), P2 (default) to P1 (high) and P0 (critical). Text can also be specified
for a substring search of description and notes.

Cmd and IDs can be swapped, multiple IDs can be specified for batch
operations.

run "dstask help <cmd>" for command specific help.

Add -- to ignore the current context. / can be used when adding tasks to note
any words after.

Available commands:

next              : Show most important tasks (priority, creation date -- truncated and default)
add               : Add a task
template          : Add a task template
log               : Log a task (already resolved)
start             : Change task status to active
note              : Append to or edit note for a task
stop              : Change task status to pending
done              : Resolve a task
context           : Set global context for task list and new tasks (use "none" to set no context)
modify            : Change task attributes specified on command line
edit              : Edit task with text editor
undo              : Undo last n commits
sync              : Pull then push to git repository, automatic merge commit.
open              : Open all URLs found in summary/annotations
git               : Pass a command to git in the repository. Used for push/pull.
remove            : Remove a task (use to remove tasks added by mistake)
show-projects     : List projects with completion status
show-tags         : List tags in use
show-active       : Show tasks that have been started
show-paused       : Show tasks that have been started then stopped
show-open         : Show all non-resolved tasks (without truncation)
show-resolved     : Show resolved tasks
show-templates    : Show task templates
show-unorganised  : Show untagged tasks with no projects (global context)
bash-completion   : Print bash completion script to stdout
fish-completion   : Print fish completion script to stdout
zsh-completion    : Print zsh completion script to stdout
help              : Get help on any command or show this message

cat > /tmp/harness.py <<'PY'
import subprocess, os, tempfile, shutil, re, json

ORIG="./executable"
MINE="/tmp/myexe"

def run(cmd, repo, env_extra={}, use_fake=False):
    env={**os.environ, 'DSTASK_GIT_REPO':repo}
    if use_fake:
        env['DSTASK_FAKE_PTY']='1'
    # remove FAKE if not use_fake?
    if not use_fake and 'DSTASK_FAKE_PTY' in env:
        del env['DSTASK_FAKE_PTY']
    env.update(env_extra)
    p=subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, env=env, text=True, input=None)
    return p.returncode, p.stdout, p.stderr

def normalize(s):
    # replace UUIDs, timestamps, commit hashes, etc. with placeholders
    s=re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', 'UUID', s)
    s=re.sub(r'20\d\d-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d(\.\d+)?Z', 'TIME', s)
    s=re.sub(r'20\d\d-\d\d-\d\d \d\d:\d\d:\d\d(\.\d+)? \+\d+ UTC', 'TIME', s)
    s=re.sub(r'\[master [0-9a-f]{7}\]','[BRANCH]', s)
    s=re.sub(r'\[master \([a-z\-]+\) [0-9a-f]{7}\]','[BRANCH]', s)
    s=re.sub(r' [0-9a-f]{7} ', ' HASH ', s)
    s=re.sub(r'pending/[0-9a-f\-]+\.yml', 'pending/UUID.yml', s)
    s=re.sub(r'resolved/[0-9a-f\-]+\.yml', 'resolved/UUID.yml', s)
    s=re.sub(r'template/[0-9a-f\-]+\.yml', 'template/UUID.yml', s)
    s=re.sub(r'active/[0-9a-f\-]+\.yml', 'active/UUID.yml', s)
    s=re.sub(r'paused/[0-9a-f\-]+\.yml', 'paused/UUID.yml', s)
    # commit messages with IDs? Keep IDs
    return s

def test_sequence(ops):
    # ops is list of (cmd, use_fake, env_extra, stdin?)
    # create two fresh repos
    import tempfile
    d1=tempfile.mkdtemp()
    d2=tempfile.mkdtemp()
    r1=os.path.join(d1,'repo')
    r2=os.path.join(d2,'repo')
    for (cmd, fake, extra, stdin_data) in ops:
        # run on both
        env1={**os.environ, 'DSTASK_GIT_REPO':r1}
        env2={**os.environ, 'DSTASK_GIT_REPO':r2}
        if fake:
            env1['DSTASK_FAKE_PTY']='1'
            env2['DSTASK_FAKE_PTY']='1'
        else:
            env1.pop('DSTASK_FAKE_PTY',None)
            env2.pop('DSTASK_FAKE_PTY',None)
        env1.update(extra); env2.update(extra)
        p1=subprocess.run([ORIG]+cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, env=env1, input=stdin_data)
        p2=subprocess.run([MINE]+cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, env=env2, input=stdin_data)
        n1=normalize(p1.stdout); n2=normalize(p2.stdout)
        e1=normalize(p1.stderr); e2=normalize(p2.stderr)
        if p1.returncode!=p2.returncode or n1!=n2 or e1!=e2:
            print(f"FAIL cmd={cmd} fake={fake} extra={extra}")
            print(f"  orig rc={p1.returncode} mine rc={p2.returncode}")
            if n1!=n2:
                print("  stdout diff:")
                print("  orig:", repr(n1[:500]))
                print("  mine:", repr(n2[:500]))
            if e1!=e2:

package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

func isTTY() bool {
	if os.Getenv("DSTASK_FAKE_PTY") != "" {
		return true
	}
	fi, err := os.Stdout.Stat()
	if err != nil {
		return false
	}
	return fi.Mode()&os.ModeCharDevice != 0
}

func confirmOrAbort(prompt string) {
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s", prompt)
	reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)
	line, err := reader.ReadString('\n')
	if err != nil {
		// original panics on EOF; we handle gracefully by aborting
		// to avoid stack trace differences, just abort
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "\x1b[31mAborted.\x1b[0m\n")
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	line = strings.TrimSpace(strings.ToLower(line))
	if line == "y" || line == "yes" {
		return
	}
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "\x1b[31mAborted.\x1b[0m\n")
	os.Exit(1)
}

func confirm(prompt string) bool {
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s", prompt)
	reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)
	line, err := reader.ReadString('\n')
	if err != nil {
		return false
	}
	line = strings.TrimSpace(strings.ToLower(line))
	return line == "y" || line == "yes"
}

func red(s string) string {
	return "\x1b[31m" + s + "\x1b[0m"
}

func yellow(s string) string {
	return "\x1b[33m" + s + "\x1b[0m"
}

func grey(s string) string {
	return "\x1b[38;5;245m" + s + "\x1b[0m"
}
